The toll books of the northern coast

How a table decides what a port can see

Harbour authorities across the northern coast have spent a decade arguing about how to count the cargo that passes through their toll booths, and the argument has never really been about the numbers themselves. The dispute is about categories: a barge carrying salt is counted differently from a barge carrying timber, a barge that unloads twice in one week is counted twice, and a shipment that is split between two quays is counted once by each quay, which flatters the totals of any port with a busy waterfront. This article follows a single clerk through one season of ledgers and shows how those categories were invented, defended and quietly revised whenever a neighbouring port published a more impressive figure. What emerges is less a record of trade than a record of institutional vanity, and a reminder that the shape of a table decides what its readers are able to see.

By Maren Holt · 14 November 2026

Introduction

The toll books were kept in a room above the customs house, and the room had one window that faced the water. Every morning the clerk opened the shutters, sharpened two pencils, and copied the previous day's entries into a fair copy that would be sent to the capital at the end of the month. The work was dull in the way that all careful work is dull, and it was easy to believe that nothing in the ledgers could be wrong, because every line had been checked by someone who had no reason to lie about a cargo of salt.

But the categories were not stable. In the spring the harbourmaster decided that barrels of pitch should be counted with the other naval stores, and by midsummer the pitch had been separated again because a rival port had begun to advertise its naval stores as a single impressive total. Nobody wrote down why the change had been made, and the clerk did not ask. He simply ruled a new column, carried the old figures across, and hoped that the auditors in the capital would be too busy to notice that the past had been rewritten in a cleaner hand.

The ledger room still exists, although the tolls are now collected by machine.
